questions.question: Define a communicable disease.
questions.modelAnswer: A disease caused by a pathogen that can be transmitted from one organism to another.
markingPoints: A disease caused by a pathogen that can be transmitted from one organism to another.

questions.question: Define a pathogen and name the four main pathogen groups.
questions.modelAnswer: A microorganism that causes infectious disease bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists.
markingPoints: A microorganism that causes infectious disease
bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists.

questions.question: Explain how bacteria can make a person ill.
questions.modelAnswer: Bacteria reproduce rapidly inside the body they may damage cells directly and/or produce toxins the toxins damage cells and tissues.
markingPoints: Bacteria reproduce rapidly inside the body
they may damage cells directly and/or produce toxins
the toxins damage cells and tissues.

questions.question: Explain how viruses can make a person ill.
questions.modelAnswer: Viruses enter living cells and use the cells' machinery to replicate new viruses are produced the host cells are damaged or destroyed.
markingPoints: Viruses enter living cells and use the cells' machinery to replicate
new viruses are produced
the host cells are damaged or destroyed.

questions.question: Compare bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists as pathogens.
questions.modelAnswer: Bacteria are living cells that reproduce rapidly and may release toxins. Viruses are non-cellular and replicate only inside host cells, damaging them. Fungi may grow on/in tissues and produce spores. Protists are single-celled eukaryotes some are parasites and may be spread by vectors.
markingPoints: Bacteria are living cells that reproduce rapidly and may release toxins. Viruses are non-cellular and replicate only inside host cells, damaging them. Fungi may grow on/in tissues and produce spores. Protists are single-celled eukaryotes
some are parasites and may be spread by vectors.

markingPoints: Air/droplets, e.g. measles

questions.question: Explain why the antibiotic with the largest inhibition zone cannot automatically be declared the best treatment for a patient.
questions.modelAnswer: Zone size depends on diffusion through agar as well as bacterial inhibition. Clinical choice also depends on safe dose, side effects, tissue reached and whether the pathogen is susceptible in the body. The plate provides supporting evidence, not a complete clinical conclusion.

questions.question: Why should an antibiotic-disc investigation include a disc containing only the solvent?
questions.modelAnswer: It is a negative control. If no clear zone forms around it, any inhibition around antibiotic discs can be attributed to the antibiotic rather than the solvent or disc.

questions.question: A plant has yellow leaves and reduced growth. Explain why these observations alone are insufficient to identify a pathogen and state two further approaches.
questions.modelAnswer: The symptoms are non-specific and could be caused by mineral deficiency or environmental stress. Compare with a gardening manual or website, examine the plant for visible pests, use test kits containing monoclonal antibodies, or send a sample for laboratory identification.
